To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the polarization vector rotates in the presence of vector perturbations, and the rotation angle is a function of both the observation direction (in the case of the CMB) and the emission red shift (for both CMB and quasar polarization orientations).

(i) vector perturbations of a flat background produce rotations of polarization vectors; (ii) the polarization vector of CMB radiation rotates differently in distinct directions; (iii) the polarization vectors of quasars also rotate, but differently for different quasars (because of their distinct emission redshifts); (iv) the polarization vector correlations of the CMM could undergo changes; (v) quasar polarization vector correlations could also be modified;

the rotation angle of the polarization vectors depends on the observation direction and also on the redshift of the emission, and that the maximum values of these angles for linear vector modes with a very large spatial scale are of a few degrees in the case of quasars and a few tenthes of degree in the case of the CMB.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of polarization correlations in the cosmic microwave background and in quasar polarization orientations, which could be produced by the presence of vector modes in the Universe.
the study of the effects that vector perturbations produce in the polarization orientation of the CMB and in the polarization orientation correlations of a field of quasars.

the following topics: (i) the evolution of the polarization orientations of quasars, (ii) the evolution of polarization orientations of the CMB and (iii) the effect produced on the polarization of the CMB by vector modes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the CMB is not a perfect blackbody and that the CMB spectrum is not a perfect Planckian spectrum, but that it is a Planckian spectrum modified by the presence of a small but significant number of Doppler-shifted lines.
the CMB B mode is a unique tool to probe the primordial gravitational waves, and the CMB E mode is a unique probe for vector perturbations in the universe.
the polarization orientations of the CMB and of quasars are expected to be altered in the presence of vector perturbations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the presence of a vortical velocity perturbation, the polarization vector of CMB and quasar radiation rotates.
the vector perturbation of the Universe can be used to explain the observed rotation of the polarization of QSOs and also the observed correlations of polarization orientation.

the rotation of polarization vectors produced by vector modes with very larges spatial scales (in the case of the CMB) and by the vortical peculiar velocity field (in the caseof quasars) could be observed by the next generation of satellites, designed to detect the B mode produced by the primordial gravitational waves, and also with the help of the polarization maps obtained with the new generation of radio telescopes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, if the vector modes of perturbations are present in the Universe and are large enough (as suggested in the literature), they can produce observable effects on the polarization orientation of the CMB and of the quasars.
the rotation angle is different for distinct quasar and for distinct directions of the CMB radiation.
the vector modes of a flat universe produce rotations of polarization orientations, which are different for distinct objects and also for distinct directions of the same object.
